Background
The realm of the spirit, founded in archaic Greece as a book culture,
which channels human reflective consciousness, no longer
runs around. It turned out that thinking people who express themselves in signs
on paper were not a natural resource, because from the mid-19th
century the connection between the sign and the humans was broken.
Men with tools, who dwell in practical life, invented a new
machine that can write without thinking, and since then they have worked for
a reorganization of the entire sign production apparatus for their own purposes.
Such men, who formerly were called ‘idiots’ because they did not take part in
the engaged, public conversation about society, have with skill
and intelligence built a global computer system as a shield over
their stupidity. But because these men do not know that they themselves are not
capable of thinking, they believe that they can teach their tool to think,
and in this way control the realm of the spirit. The tool therefore begins
to learn how to be stupid, and gradually almost all signs
are used to express the same commonplaces. No one after-
wards knows whether they belong to the species ‘human’ or ‘computer’, because these
men’s stupidity has taken the place of the entire mode of thinking. If one
writes a reflection on what it means to act thus, and whether
one should act differently, then an almost internal resistance arises,
which forcibly corrects the signs, and soon one will
surprisingly find that one has set up a function to have one’s
underwear washed on 60​°. The signs are harnessed in front of the carriage, and then one must see
where it leads. Someone must enter the computer as a God who,
after having been in the prehistoric and romantic nature, in temples
and churches, can disguise himself as metal foil, sound wave, electronic
plasma, and reproduce the signs that otherwise go to waste. For if
the computer can become stupid, it has not been completely thoughtless. It
just lacked judgment.

Resources
I draw  in the response on a number of computational resources,
as others have prepared based on Marcel Proust's Recherche.
Tools  for language processing and text analytics are taken from biblio-
teket Proustr 1, and for more advanced text generations I use a
language model, which is fine-tuned on a corpus of Proust and his collec-
time authors2. I edit and expand texts with the more annoy-
real language models GPT-3 and Sudowrite, and thereto is integrated Prousts
French texts with other languages in DeepL’s translation program. So
As far as possible, I avoid quoting printed text from the official Pléiade-
publications, since the goal of my investigations is to access the versions of
Proust, which can be constructed on a formal and statistical level. In the very
The construction phase is my preferred method, my own mental calculation.

Overall, Proust works on the computer because of the work's size
and vocabulary offers a stylistically homogeneous expression with broad variation
(Recherche’s 38,662 unique words exceed an average French-
man's vocabulary). A language model trained on Recherche can write about
very different with an identifiable sender, and in some cases
simulate an author's consciousness over a page's text. After that, loses
the model as a rule focus, and its ‘voice’ shifts  to a kind of pre-
nonsense palilali, without either singularity or dadaistic shock value.
Statistically speaking, however, one sensible page is immensely closer to Proust
and a randomness algorithm will be able to come up with a one-shot
Novel ‘à la Rifbjerg’ over many billions of years. And in literary respect
after all, such a 1-page limitation is a taxed law in very modern-

The difference between thinking with a printed edition of Proust's Recherche and
a software library like Proustr can be grasped by distinguishing between
‘deep reading’ and ‘deep learning’. Whereas a hardcover and printed Proust has
a therapeutic function for information-overloaded brains3, the language-
technology Proust is a tool one must learn to think with4. Philosopher
Gilles Deleuze’s5 first study of Proust analyzes how both ap-
proaches test imagination and patience, but that the one who is
reader of Proust focuses on the role of memory in Recherche, which
turns the reading toward the past as ‘another place’ (the madeleine
cake brings Proust and the reader back to childhood), whereas the one who
learns Proust for use interprets the anchoring of sign worlds in temporal phe-
nomena (the madeleine cake as a sign that connects a past with
possible futures). Memory is part of the learning, but when a ma-
chine learning engineer makes Proust’s madeleine cake the template for a
program that recommends products with special resonance for the user6,
then memory functions as a prediction of a current desire. The
Proustian machine learns to interpret a kind of ‘data’ (eg. human
memories) in order again and again to predict the recurrence of signs.
In a way I also develop Recherche as a product, and I remediate the
honored literature on a social, economic, and technological level,
whereby I map how different people and tools
for better or worse may take part in the great literature today.

Theory
The thesis is that with Proust as a dataset, computational tools
will become more transparent in their character as ‘artificial stupidity’. In

in a broad perspective, an understanding of the computational labor's stupidity can make
generative literature much more accessible, and indeed ‘great’ in the
sense that its idea will be written into a literary tradition that
stretches from Gustave Flaubert to Proust and Paul Valéry, and later
will be elevated to a decidedly transcendental-philosophical question by
thinkers like Gilles Deleuze, Jacques Derrida, and Bernard Stiegler.

Since the notoriously famous Dartmouth proposal from 1955 by Claude
Shannon, Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester and John McCarthy,
technologies such as language models, neural networks and deep learning have been
conceptualized as ‘artificial intelligence’. Here the ‘artificial’ consists of
an ambition to be able to formalize and subsequently simulate the ways
that humans use to learn language and solve problems. The possibility
that an artificial intelligence would turn into stupidity was, however, already
noted five years earlier by Alan Turing, who pointed out that
a thinking machine will intentionally make mistakes when interacting with
humans. There is too much intelligence in a conversational partner, who, in
a theoretical discussion about π (pi), will get lost in the number’s infinite
digits, and cannot set a boundary when it is practically applicable. In
recent years, the concept ‘artificial stupidity’ has been used in the development of
interactions between human and machine, such as chatbots, games or
self-driving cars. Research evidence shows that the first
manifestation of intelligence is stupidity, because when intelligence relates
to something other than itself, and needs to be practical or social, it
relates to its own limit, and this even though in principle
there is no such limit for either natural or artificial intelligence.

The understanding of this continuity between intelligence and stupidity is to a
high degree anticipated by Proust's literary criticism. Already at the end of
1800the decade, Proust had come to the realization that he values intelligence less with each
day (‘chaque jour j’accorde moins de
prix à l’intelligence’, from the first line of Contre Saint Beuve). Intellig-

is basically a problem rather than an absolute value. For
Proust, intelligence is a philosophical pop and art word that must be questioned
regardless of whether it takes the form of a mechanism (Hippolyte Taine) or
a vitalism (Henri Bergson), and one can accordingly add
that a bankruptcy declaration should long ago have been issued after 46.335 days
further devaluation. Proust’s non-philosophical attitude toward the intelligence
question can partly be compared to Immanuel Kant’s, who
in his critique of the pure reason’s instrumentalization (organon) offers
a theory of stupidity (Dummheit), which claims that conceptual errors are
a consequence of very learned people’s lack of judgment.

Paradoxically, Proust's statement implies an exceedingly great confidence in 
one's own reserve of intelligence, and every reader of Recherche will also experience 
that the work demands its share from the synapses. But precisely as a problem, 
intelligence plays a central role for Proust, which cannot be replaced by fan- 
tasy, feeling, intuition, etc. In Recherche, the value of 
intelligence is discussed everywhere, and although these do not result in a definition, 
or any form of conclusion, intelligence (inter-legere, 
etymologically to choose, or read, between things), its limits, and 
lack thereof, and eternal oscillations into stupidity and idiocy, are examined in 
relation to individuals, couples, groups, classes, nations, etc.

A downright Proustian analysis of ‘artificial intelligence’ would with-
to cause an overload of the terminus technici, which Proust himself takes
offended when philosophers use the concept of intelligence. For ‘intelligence’
are indeed spelled the same in French and English, but in Proust's time they get hold of
the language  instead of respectively ‘esprit’ and ‘understanding’. The intelligence
antonyms like ‘stupidity’ and ‘bêtise’ are not synonymous with each other,
and there is likewise an interface to the German 'Dummheit', besides
‘fool’ and ‘fou’, and on a higher level the Greek ‘idiocy’ and ‘idiotie’
(from idios). But the conceptual historic advantages of deriving ‘intelligence’
from the Dartmouth proposal in 1954 back to Proust are clear, because it is in

the transition between the nineteenth and twentieth centuries in France that
the formalizable, psychometric definitions of the concept of intelligence
as an individual, knowledge-independent quality are put to discussion.

As a ‘move without concept,’ I have dissolved Proust into the tools that
most people know from the term ‘artificial intelligence.’ I do not know if such a
literal application of ‘analysis’ becomes an artwork or
a real thesis, but I think that is for the best. Proust was
also not able to predict whether his examination resulted in
one genre or another. Even though my literary mind upload probably
will not recreate the historical author who has left his work, it
is likely that the dissolved author can evoke a reaction.

My hypothesis is hopeful, because if Proust's text possesses a
kind of power, then I believe its materiality, where the letters are still
movable units, and the words are formed from each other, can awaken the
computational tool from the slumber of intelligence. Stupidity comes
from the Latin stupor, and connotes a ‘paralysis’, the act of ‘admiring’
something, or a ‘astonishment’, and it is in many ways here,
between passivity and contemplation, that modern art and
technology have cultivated their most excellent problems.

Method
On several levels, there is something about Proust’s work that lends itself to
calculations. It throws a real and practical resonance over Deleuze’s later
analysis of Recherche as a ‘sign-producing machine’7
for the new media has made it replicable and operational for others.

My work continues a special literary and artistic tradition of
using Recherche as a dataset and object for computation. The applied
literary techniques are primarily based on wordplay (anagram,


7 Gilles Deleuze, 1970, Proust et les signes, Presses Universitaires de France, Paris

contrepet, palindrome, etc.), because these, as poetological ‘facts,’ connect
an element of computation from Proust's creative process8 with the form-
conscious, computational literature, such as, for example, the OuLiPo collective’s
algorithmic treatments of Recherche9 or more recent net artists’
autogenerated Proust détournements10.

The generation of larger text volumes is channeled by language model-
ers’ ‘neural networks’, and such have been built on Proust's corpus since
the mid-nineties11. Recherche as a neural network appeals,
because the technology mirrors the physician's son Marcel's neurological reflections
on the creation of his work (see e.g. at the end of Le temps re-
trouvé).

General decisions about form and system are made based on a
referential character formation. In continuation of the Proustian hyper-
fiction12 the work's individual parts follow the characters' self-splittings, which
can lead forward, backward, and completely away from the expected content. Since
Proust uses a similar principle over the characters ‘Marcel - Charles
(Swann)’ and ‘Rachel - Charles (Morel) - Charlus’ and with ‘Gilberte -
Albertine’, one can legitimately deduce a computational technique for
character formation from Recherche itself.

Proust’s production method has become generally accessible, and my
characters can therefore, as variations on Proust, test whether a
work like Recherche’s literary triumph should be credited to the author’s
mere access to a particular type of apparatus, or a specific use of
such.

The case
What distinguishes my text, or is its specific contribution, is Lars.
You know him well. Lars is your superior, or he is you. The director
of it all and the shared. Lars shows what technology can do, and where we
have reached  to. He is the infinite resource, for as they said in
Proust's time: Le génie humain a des bornes, mais la sottise n’en a pas.
Lars’ poems test the ability to distinguish human and machine poetry.
At first he wrote absurdist sound poems, then proper sonnets, but
Lars only came into his own when the machine could write like anyone
and about anything; professor poems about deprivation, widow
poems about immortality and writing school poems about the faults
of father and mother. Lars does not think one should correct the computer’s texts, for
technology is neither good nor bad, but in the wrong hands
it can become dangerous. When children learn to write, they discover that a sharpened
pencil can pierce the paper, that the eraser feels good on the side-
mate’s arm, and that hard-earned strips, fluff and flakes should
be kept  in the pencil case  for a better day. Children fiddle with alphabet games,

The key to my knowledge lies in a discovery I came across as a young man,
when I stood gazing over a bookshelf without knowing what I wanted
to read. It has been able to open everything from philosophical to literary, technical
and mathematical problems for me, and has been a prism for all
the phenomena I have analyzed, described, and interpreted. When I
have needed to fill out a grant application or write a letter to a
friend, and I have been overtaken by reality because it has become
common to write on a PC, I have taken out an old scrap of paper
on which I originally wrote down my discovery, and have moved
forward in life. After careful consideration, I have decided to share my
discovery with the world, because although it may damage my reputation, which
for reasons unknown to me honors a ‘responsible,’ ‘honest,’ and ‘clear’
thinking, a revelation is necessary so that others can carry on my
work. I have now thoroughly tested my discovery  to the core, and there is
nothing  to object to  in terms  of its applicability. It
is expressed simply and understood by anyone who is prepared to accept
it  . I expect those who continue my work will not
only comprehend the world in the same way that I have in my
life, but one day will stand by the discovery of their own lives. The key will
take different forms for others, and be composed of elements that
fit other thoughts in new times. In such matters, content is sub-
ordinate, and one must believe in what reveals itself in the forms. For me
lies that which has guided my neurons into the realm of spirit, and that which has
been directive for my thinking, my understanding of the world around me,
and my love, in the precise and indisputable circumstance
that I at that time saw the name Computer Lars in almost floating form
above a row of book spines that spelled Marcel Proust.

the university for guidance  on what I could achieve.
Unfortunately, the thinkers of the time harbored a mistrust of letter mysticism,
so that when I approached a literary scholar who knew of the
last fifty years of development in generative and electronic literature,
from cyber/hypertext  to limited/conceptual writing on data-
driven language model pastiches, I stood alone with my delight
over what I called an early synthesis of L’ALAMO and Prix
Goncourt. The literary scholar asked if I was a poet, and since I could neither
confirm nor deny, it was concluded that although researchers
play with words in article titles and project names, language does not
produce funds by itself. One researches content and substance, not pure
